opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think a year ago a lot of us, myself included, were quite optimistic. The feeling was that once we had decent hardware and enough teleoperation setups, data would just start accumulating, and we'd see the same kind of scaling story we saw with language and vision. That hasn't really happened, at least not at the pace I hoped.

A few things stand out. First, the cost. Collecting real-world robot data is still extremely expensive. You need the robot, the operator, the environment, the resets, the maintenance. When you calculate the cost per useful trajectory, it's orders of magnitude higher than scraping text or images. So even well-funded teams end up with datasets that are, by internet standards, tiny.

Second, the data is very fragmented. Every lab and company has its own embodiment, its own gripper, its own camera placement, its own action space. So even when people do share data, it doesn't combine as cleanly as we'd like. You can't simply pool it and expect a model to generalize across all of it. We talk about cross-embodiment a lot, but in practice it's still hard.

Third, and maybe this is the most important, there's a quality and diversity problem. A lot of the data being collected is repetitive: the same tasks in similar scenes, often in lab settings. It looks like a big number of hours, but the actual information content is not that rich. What we really need is long-tail diversity, different objects, lighting, failures, recoveries, and that's exactly the hardest thing to get through teleoperation.

And then simulation, which many hoped would fill the gap, still has the sim-to-real issue, especially for contact-rich manipulation. Rendering has gotten much better, but physics, materials, deformable objects, those are still far from reality.

So my disappointment isn't that nobody is working on it. Lots of people are. It's more that we haven't found the paradigm shift, something like what the internet was for language, a cheap, scalable, naturally occurring source of data. Personally I think the answer will involve learning much more from human video and world models, and treating robot data as the final alignment step rather than the main source. But we're not there yet, and that's why the past year felt slower than I expected.

r001.rationale: The response says the field has not found a paradigm shift or a cheap, scalable data source, but it does not attribute weaker urgency to a lack of embodied-native developments over the past year.

r002.rationale: It discusses the high cost and small size of robot datasets, but does not state that immediate pressure to collect large volumes exists only for foundation-model training.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a year ago I thought data would be the thing that broke open for embodied AI the way it did for language and vision. I was fairly optimistic. And looking back, the progress on data has been slower than I expected, for a few reasons.

The first is just the physics of collection. With language, the internet already existed; the data was sitting there, and the cost of consuming it was almost zero. With embodied data, every single trajectory has to be produced in the physical world, by a person operating a robot, or by a robot acting in a real environment. There's no free lunch. You can't crawl it. So the scale is bounded by how many robots, how many operators, how many hours. Everybody understood this intellectually, but I think many of us, myself included, underestimated how hard the ramp actually is once you try to go from a few thousand episodes to millions.

The second issue is quality and consistency, which I think is underrated. A lot of the data collected this past year is not really reusable across embodiments or even across labs. Different robots, different cameras, different action spaces, different annotation conventions. So even when the raw volume looks like it's going up, the effective, mergeable data is much smaller. In vision we had ImageNet as a shared target. In embodied, we still don't have a widely accepted standard for what a "good" dataset looks like, and that fragmentation is costing us.

The third thing is the simulation-to-real gap. I had hoped that simulation and generative world models would substitute for a large fraction of real-world collection by now. They help, especially for pretraining and for visual diversity, but the contact-rich parts, the manipulation, the friction, the deformable objects, those are still where simulated data falls apart. So the shortcut I was counting on turned out to be narrower than expected.

And there's a more structural problem, which is incentives. The companies that have the robots and can collect data at scale treat that data as their moat. So very little of it flows into the open research community. Academic groups end up building small, bespoke datasets, and the field doesn't compound the way it did when large open datasets were the norm.

So to be clear, I don't think the direction is wrong. I still believe data is the bottleneck and the opportunity. I just think the timeline I had in my head was too aggressive. The honest assessment is that we've made progress on model architecture and on demos, but the data layer, the thing that actually determines whether these systems generalize, is maybe a year or two behind where I thought it would be.

r001.rationale: The response explains slower-than-expected progress through collection limits, inconsistent data, simulation gaps, and incentives. It does not attribute weaker urgency to a lack of embodied-native developments.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that pressure to acquire very large data volumes depends on training a foundation model.

astra-6.text:
I think the main gap is between collecting more data and collecting data that actually improves a robot’s capabilities. We expected that once more teams started collecting embodied data, we would see a clear cycle: more data, better models, broader deployment, and then even more useful data. My impression is that this cycle has been slower to develop than we hoped.

In robotics, an episode is tied to a particular robot, environment, and task. You can collect a lot of demonstrations, but if they’re repetitive or too specific to one setup, the model may not learn much that transfers elsewhere. So the volume can grow without a corresponding improvement in generalization.

There’s also the feedback problem. When a model fails, can we identify what data is missing, collect it, and reliably show that the new data fixes the failure? Without that loop, it’s difficult to know whether we’re making progress or simply accumulating recordings.

So what has fallen short of my expectations isn’t just the amount of data. It’s how quickly we’re learning to turn that data into dependable capabilities. I’d like to see more emphasis on that whole process, from collection through evaluation.

r001.rationale: The response says the data-to-capability feedback cycle has been slower than expected, but does not attribute weaker urgency for large data volumes to a lack of embodied-native developments.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that large-scale data acquisition lacks immediate pressure outside foundation-model training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I underestimated how difficult it would be to turn collected data into useful learning signals. A robot can run for hours and generate a lot of video, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve collected many examples that help it learn a new skill.

In embodied tasks, the details matter: what the robot observes, what action it takes, and what happens afterward. When a demonstration fails, was it a perception problem, a control problem, or simply a bad demonstration? If you can’t distinguish those cases, collecting more data may just give you more ambiguity.

There’s also the question of transfer. Data collected with one robot, one gripper, or one setup may have limited value when any of those things change. So the amount of data can grow while the capabilities improve much more slowly.

What I had hoped to see was a stronger feedback loop: collect data, train a model, identify where it fails, and use those failures to guide the next round of collection. My disappointment is less about the volume of data than about how difficult it still is to make that loop work reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says large amounts of data may not improve skills, but does not attribute the weaker urgency to a lack of embodied-native developments over the past year.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention foundation-model training or state that there is no concrete pressure to acquire very large volumes of data immediately.
